title: Kernel scheduler stress sandbox
content:
TL;DR:
Quick sandbox log of stress experiments that exercise kernel selection thrash + KV-cache churn across mixed sequence-length workloads. Goal was to produce high-fidelity traces we can replay in ProbeBench for tail latency regressions and to capture indicators that our scheduler heuristics are unstable when KV shard eviction crosses a kernel boundary.

Context and motivation:
- We keep seeing intermittent 99.9th latency spikes in canary runs for llama-variant models when sequence-length distribution shifts (more long prompts + many short completions). Hypothesis: scheduler switches kernels (FP16 -> int4 path) while KV-cache population and shard evictions are being processed, creating lock contention and hot-path copies.
- Existing microbench harnesses test kernels and kvcache independently; this sandbox intentionally mixes them with a tiny stateful workload to reproduce real-world tail behavior.

Harness architecture (short):
- Driver: sandbox-driver (python) that sends interleaved requests with a configurable mix: {short:50%, medium:30%, long:20%} and injects synthetic prefix-sharing groups to exercise KV reuse + eviction.
- Server: instrumented dev build (runtime/branch: feature/kernel-switch-trace) with extra tracing points around scheduler_accept(), kernel_bind(), kvcache_evict(), and worker_backpressure().
- Trace sink: local jaeger-compatible collector + binary trace dumps for replay. We tag traces with scenario id and seed.

Experiment matrix (what we ran):
- Seeds: 3 per row (deterministic rng seed in driver).
- Kernel profiles: baseline (no-quant), fp16-fast, int4-agg, hybrid-switch (heuristic).
- KV configs: small-shard (64MB/shard), medium-shard (256MB), aggressive-evict (LRU threshold 0.6).
- Scheduler modes: conservative-batch, aggressive-batch, latency-first (single-request fast-path).

Important commands (how to reproduce locally):
- start server: ./bin/runtime --config configs/dev-sandbox.yaml --trace-out /tmp/traces/s1 --branch feature/kernel-switch-trace
- driver: python tools/sandbox-driver.py --mix 50,30,20 --kv-grouping 0.7 --duration 600 --seed 42 --collector http://localhost:14268/api/traces
- replay: tools/probebench replay --trace /tmp/traces/s1/seed42.bin --target local-dev --verify-metrics

Observed signals and quick interpretations:
1) Tail latency correlation with kvcache_evict spikes:
- When eviction_count/sec > 120, 99.9th latency jumps by 2.3-3.1x compared to baseline.
- Correlation stronger in hybrid-switch kernel profile; likely because eviction callback path holds scheduler lock while kernel selection logic probes model metadata.

2) Kernel thrash window:
- We observed repeated kernel_bind()/kernel_unbind() flapping within a 30–80ms window during bursts.
- Each bind/unbind sequence increased CPU sys-time on host by ~7% and caused queue head-of-line blocking for short requests.

3) KV shard hotness + shard migration:
- In medium-shard config, hot prefixes concentrated on 10% of shards; when those shards hit the eviction threshold, eviction sweeps caused a cascade of cache-invalidations noticed by the worker threads.
- Cascade frequently co-occurred with kernel selection changes (hybrid), amplifying tail.

Representative microbench numbers (sanitized):
- Baseline (no-quant, conservative-batch, medium-shard): p50=18ms p95=57ms p99=118ms p999=320ms
- Hybrid-switch + aggressive-evict: p50=22ms p95=95ms p99=380ms p999=1250ms
- Int4-agg + latency-first + small-shard: p50=16ms p95=70ms p99=210ms p999=540ms
Notes: absolute values depend heavily on host GPU and sequence composition; numbers above are from a c6g-nvme-rt dev rig and meant only for relative comparison.

Trace examples to inspect (ids):
- s1-seed42: long request blocked 72ms between kernel_bind request and actual kernel entry; stack shows scheduler lock contention with kvcache evict worker (trace span ids included in dump).
- s1-seed47: repeated small requests show burst amplification where one long completion creates a stall and following shorts queue up, p99 tail climbs.

Hypotheses and root-cause notes:
- Kernel binding currently takes a global mutex to serialize kernel metadata access; if eviction runs on the same thread or acquires order-inverted locks, we get deadlock windows and latency amplification.
- Heuristic that switches to int4 when predicted tokens/sec > X does not account for KV eviction cost; we should penalize kernel switch during active eviction phases.

Quick mitigation ideas (fast experiments):
- Reduce kernel bind critical section: move metadata validation out and make binding job asynchronous (enqueue a bind request that completes while requests can still run on previous kernel until next refill). (low-risk, medium effort)
- Add eviction-aware backoff to kernel-switch heuristic: if eviction_count/sec > threshold then score switch lower. (low effort)
- Stagger eviction sweeps across shards instead of sweeping all hot shards synchronously. (medium effort)
- Introduce per-worker KV eviction queues so eviction work doesn't happen on scheduler main thread. (higher effort)

Planned follow-ups and experiments:
- A/B: implement eviction-aware backoff in scheduler heuristic and re-run matrix (target: reduce p999 by 30% in hybrid-switch configs). Tracking ticket: ENG-1254.
- Microprobe: add microprobe that artificially induces shard eviction at precise times relative to kernel bind to measure worst-case stall. (instrumented by Diego).
- Trace heartbeat: add light-weight span in scheduler that records kvcache stats snapshot at bind time for subsequent correlation.

Regression tracker (log):
- 2025-01-20: reproduced p999 blowups in hybrid-switch with medium-shard + conservative-batch. Attached trace s1-seed42. (Aisha)
- 2025-01-22: added eviction_count logging and confirmed correlation; created ENG-1254. (Priya)
- 2025-01-27: implemented temporary backoff in heuristic (branch: sandbox/evict-backoff) — initial runs show p999 reduction ~18% in noisy seeds. (Jin)

Open questions / unresolved:
- Are there model-specific allocation patterns (e.g., cross-attention kv size) that make some kernels more eviction-sensitive? Need per-model microbench.
- How much of observed flapping is due to hardware scheduler preemption vs runtime lock design? Need low-level perf tools (perf, nsight) on repro hosts.
- Should we consider a single long-lived int4 worker pool for smaller requests to avoid bind churn entirely? (tradeoffs with quantization quality)

Appendix: quick trace grep snippets used:
- grep "kvcache_evict" /tmp/traces/s1/seed42.log | wc -l -> 847 evictions in 10m run
- jq '.spans[]|select(.operation=="kernel_bind")|.duration' seed42.json | sort -n | tail -n 20 -> many in 40-80ms bucket during burst windows

TODOs (short):
- [ ] Create reproducible microprobe script and attach to ENG-1254 (owner: Diego)
- [ ] Prototype eviction-aware switch scoring in scheduler (owner: Jin)
- [ ] Add lightweight kv stats span at kernel bind (owner: Aisha)
- [ ] Run full matrix on dedicated perf cluster and upload traces to S3 (owner: Priya)

Notes to self / rough ideas:
- Might be useful to have a small in-memory KV emulator in driver that mimics eviction bursts so we can test without changing server eviction code.
- Consider adding a "no-bind-window" flag to accept new requests without binding if current pending evictions > X (fast toggle for canary).

References and links:
- runtime PR with extra tracing: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/893
- ENG ticket: ENG-1254 (kernel-scheduler/eviction-regression)
- ProbeBench replay tool: tools/probebench (see README in repo)

End of sandbox log.

(Informal: this is a living notebook — expect more experimental results and rough traces to be appended here as we iterate.)
